title: The Kerberos Network Authentication Service (V5)
subtitle: How you prove who you are to many servers while typing your password once and never sending it.
summary: Kerberos lets a client and a server on an untrusted network prove their identities to each other through a trusted third party, the Key Distribution Center (KDC). The user logs in once to get a ticket-granting ticket, then trades it for per-service tickets without re-entering a password, and the password never crosses the network. RFC 4120 is the full Version 5 specification and replaces RFC 1510.

eli5.summary: Imagine a theme park where you show your ID once at the front gate and get a wristband. After that, every ride checks the wristband instead of asking for your ID again, and you never hand your ID to a ride operator.

questions: what is a ticket granting ticket
what is the difference between as-req and tgs-req
why does kerberos need synchronized clocks
what is a kerberos realm and principal

tldr.problem: Sending a password to every server you use is unsafe, and servers cannot trust a client's claim about who it is.
tldr.mechanism: A trusted KDC issues a ticket-granting ticket after a login, then issues service tickets that carry a fresh session key. The client proves it holds that key by sending an authenticator containing a timestamp.
tldr.outcome: One login gives access to many services without the password or long-term keys crossing the network. It is the basis of Active Directory authentication and many Unix and Hadoop deployments.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.content:
Kerberos is a network authentication service. A client wants to talk to a server, and each side needs to be sure of the other's identity, even though the network between them may be watched or tampered with. The two parties do not already share a secret. Instead, each shares a secret key with a trusted third party, the Key Distribution Center (KDC).

The KDC is described as two logical services: the Authentication Service (AS) and the Ticket-Granting Service (TGS). The RFC notes that in practice they are "different protocol entry points within a single Kerberos server." The client first asks the AS for a ticket-granting ticket (TGT). It later presents the TGT to the TGS to get a ticket for a particular application server. Only then does it contact that server.

Two things make the design work. A ticket is a record the client cannot read or forge, encrypted in the target server's key. An authenticator is a small encrypted timestamp the client builds with the shared session key to show it is the ticket's rightful holder. The document also covers integrity-protected and encrypted application messages (KRB_SAFE and KRB_PRIV), credential forwarding (KRB_CRED), and cross-realm operation.

Kerberos provides authentication, not authorization. A valid ticket proves who the client is; the application still decides what that principal may do.
sections.eli5: Two strangers cannot trust each other directly, but both trust the same helper. The helper hands the visitor a sealed note that only the other stranger can open, so each knows the other is real.

sections.title: Principals, Realms and Tickets
sections.content:
Everything in Kerberos is named. A principal is a client or a service, written as a realm plus a name made of one or more components. A realm is an administrative domain with its own KDC and database; by convention Internet-style realm names are upper-case versions of DNS names. The ticket-granting service has a reserved principal whose name has the first component krbtgt, for example ("krbtgt", "ATHENA.MIT.EDU").

A Ticket is an application-tagged ASN.1 structure with four fields: tkt-vno (always 5), realm, sname (the service) and enc-part. The encrypted part, EncTicketPart, holds the flags, the fresh session key, the client's realm and name (crealm, cname), the transited list of realms crossed, and the times authtime, starttime, endtime and renew-till. It can also carry client addresses and authorization data.

Ticket flags are a bit field numbered 0 to 13: forwardable, forwarded, proxiable, proxy, may-postdate, postdated, invalid, renewable, initial, pre-authent, hw-authent, and the two added since RFC 1510, transited-policy-checked and ok-as-delegate. Flags let a ticket be renewed, postdated, forwarded to another host, or used by a proxy.
sections.eli5: Every person and every service gets a name tag that also says which club they belong to. A ticket is a sealed envelope with that name tag inside, plus a secret password that is good for one visit.

sections.title: The Authentication Service Exchange
sections.content:
The first exchange gets the client its initial ticket, usually a TGT. The client sends KRB_AS_REQ (application tag 10) to the AS. It is sent in the clear and contains the client name (cname), realm, requested service name (sname, usually the TGS), the requested expiry till, a random nonce, and an etype list of encryption types in preference order.

The KDC looks up the client. If the principal is unknown it returns KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN. Otherwise it replies with KRB_AS_REP (tag 11). The reply contains the ticket, encrypted in the TGS's key, and an encrypted part addressed to the client, encrypted in the client's secret key. That part carries the new session key and echoes the nonce. For a user, the key is derived from the password, so only someone who knows the password can decrypt the reply and recover the session key.

Because anyone can ask for a reply for any principal, a realm should demand pre-authentication. The KDC then answers the first request with KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED and METHOD-DATA naming the accepted methods. The client retries with a PA-ENC-TIMESTAMP, a timestamp encrypted in the client key. Section 10 states that without pre-authentication an attacker can collect ciphertext for offline password guessing.

The password itself is never transmitted. It is used locally to derive the key that unlocks the reply.
sections.eli5: You tell the front gate your name. The gate gives you a wristband locked with a lock that only your own secret can open. If you really are you, you can open it. Nobody else can.

sections.title: The Ticket-Granting Service Exchange
sections.content:
With a TGT in hand, the client asks for tickets to individual services. It sends KRB_TGS_REQ (tag 12), which has the same KDC-REQ layout as the AS request but now names the target service in sname. The padata field carries a PA-TGS-REQ, which is an ordinary AP-REQ containing the TGT and an authenticator. This is how the client proves to the TGS that it holds the TGT's session key.

The KDC checks the TGT and authenticator, then returns KRB_TGS_REP (tag 13). The reply holds a new ticket for the service, encrypted in the service's key, and a copy of the new service session key encrypted in the TGT's session key (or an authenticator subkey if the client supplied one). The client's password is not involved again.

This is the point of the two-step design. The user's long-term key is used once, at login. After that, only short-lived session keys are used. A client can also use the TGS to get a ticket for a service in another realm, passing through intermediate realms linked by inter-realm keys, and the ticket records the realms it traversed in its transited field.

AS exchange
Password-derived key, used once at login. Result: a TGT.
TGS exchange
TGT session key. Result: a service ticket, no password needed.
sections.eli5: Once you have the wristband, you show it at a booth and get a little ticket for each ride you want. You never have to prove who you are from scratch again.

sections.title: The Client/Server Exchange and Mutual Authentication
sections.content:
To use a service, the client sends it KRB_AP_REQ (tag 14). It holds ap-options, the service ticket, and an authenticator encrypted with the ticket's session key. The authenticator contains the client's realm and name, cusec and ctime (the client's clock), and optionally a checksum, a subkey and a sequence number.

The server decrypts the ticket with its own long-term key and recovers the session key. It decrypts the authenticator with that key. It then compares the names, checks the client address if the ticket has one, and checks that ctime is within the allowable clock skew. The RFC gives "e.g., 5 minutes"; otherwise it returns KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW. It must also reject authenticators it has already seen, with KRB_AP_ERR_REPEAT, which normally means keeping a replay cache.

If the client set the mutual-required option, the server returns KRB_AP_REP (tag 15). It encrypts the client's ctime and cusec in the session key. Only a server that could decrypt the ticket would know the key, so a correct reply proves the server's identity as well.

Kerberos needs loosely synchronized clocks. A host whose clock drifts beyond the skew limit will fail authentication even with a valid ticket and password.
sections.eli5: The ride operator opens your ticket with a special key and checks that the time you wrote on your note matches the clock. The operator then sends back a note only the real operator could write, so you know the ride is real too.

sections.title: Protected Messages and Credential Forwarding
sections.content:
Authentication alone does not protect what comes next. RFC 4120 therefore defines three optional application-level messages that use the session key or a negotiated subkey.

KRB_SAFE (tag 20) carries user data with a keyed checksum: it gives integrity, but the data is not hidden. KRB_PRIV (tag 21) encrypts the data and gives both privacy and integrity. Both carry timestamps or sequence numbers for replay and reordering protection, so errors such as KRB_AP_ERR_MODIFIED, KRB_AP_ERR_REPEAT and KRB_AP_ERR_BADORDER can arise. KRB_CRED (tag 22) transfers tickets and their session keys to another host, which is how credentials are forwarded.

The RFC also describes user-to-user authentication (ENC-TKT-IN-SKEY), where the service has no long-term key and the ticket is encrypted in the service's TGT session key.

Section 10 is blunt: completing the AP-REQ and AP-REP exchange without further protection gives only authentication, not confidentiality or integrity of what follows. Applications must use KRB_PRIV or KRB_SAFE, or their own protection that is securely linked to the authentication step. Many real applications use the GSS-API wrapper described in RFC 4121 instead of calling these messages directly.
sections.eli5: Showing your ticket only proves who you are. If you then want to whisper or sign a letter, there are special envelopes for that. Some seal the letter shut, and some just add a stamp that shows no one changed it.

sections.title: Message Encoding, Errors and Transport
sections.content:
All Kerberos messages are defined in ASN.1 and encoded with the Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER). Each top-level message has a fixed application tag: 1 Ticket, 10 AS-REQ, 11 AS-REP, 12 TGS-REQ, 13 TGS-REP, 14 AP-REQ, 15 AP-REP, 20 KRB-SAFE, 21 KRB-PRIV, 22 KRB-CRED and 30 KRB-ERROR. Times are GeneralizedTime with no fractional seconds, for example 19851106210627Z. Encrypted data is an EncryptedData structure with etype, an optional key version kvno, and the cipher. The key is combined with a key usage number (for example 3 for the encrypted part of an AS-REP and 11 for an AP-REQ authenticator) so one key never encrypts two kinds of message the same way.

Failures return KRB-ERROR (tag 30) with an error-code such as 6 (KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN), 25 (KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED), 32 (KRB_AP_ERR_TKT_EXPIRED), 34 (KRB_AP_ERR_REPEAT) or 37 (KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW).

KDCs must accept requests over both UDP and TCP and should listen on port 88. A UDP exchange uses one datagram each way. If the reply is too big the KDC returns KRB_ERR_RESPONSE_TOO_BIG (52), and the client retries over TCP. Clients should find KDCs using DNS SRV records such as _kerberos._udp.EXAMPLE.COM.
sections.eli5: Every kind of message has a number on the front so the receiver knows what it is. Small notes go by postcard, and if the note is too big the sender has to use a proper package instead.

sections.title: Interoperability and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Section 8 defines a minimal profile, Specification 2. Implementations must support both UDP and TCP, the encryption type AES256-CTS-HMAC-SHA1-96 from RFC 3962 with its checksum, the PA-ENC-TIMESTAMP client method, ETYPE-INFO2, DOMAIN-X500-COMPRESS transited encoding, and mutual authentication. DES-CBC-MD5 and 3DES are only "SHOULD" and the RFC warns that single DES is weak. The recommended KDC defaults are a 1-day maximum ticket lifetime, a 1-week maximum renewable lifetime, a 5-minute minimum lifetime and 5-minute clock skew.

Section 10 lists what Kerberos does not solve. The KDC database holds every principal's key, so a compromised KDC compromises its whole realm. Denial of service is not addressed, and a Kerberos outage can take down every service that depends on it. Password guessing is not prevented, because ciphertext under a password-derived key allows an offline dictionary attack. The RFC strongly encourages pre-authentication and randomly generated keys for service principals. Principal names must not be quickly recycled, or a new principal inherits stale ACL entries. A server that loses its replay cache must reject requests until the clock-skew window has passed.

Proper decryption of an AS-REP does not prove the KDC is genuine. To verify a login, a local service should obtain a service ticket and complete an AP exchange with it.
sections.eli5: The helper's big book of secrets must be guarded very carefully, and weak secrets like easy passwords can still be guessed. The clocks also need to roughly agree, or a good ticket will look too old or too new.

messages.label: KRB_AS_REQ (10)
messages.note: Who I am, which service (the TGS), a nonce, accepted etypes.

messages.label: KRB_AS_REP (11)
messages.note: TGT plus a session key sealed in the client's key.

messages.label: KRB_TGS_REQ (12)
messages.note: TGT and an authenticator, naming the target service.

messages.label: KRB_TGS_REP (13)
messages.note: Service ticket plus the service session key.

messages.label: KRB_AP_REQ (14)
messages.note: Service ticket and authenticator with a timestamp.

messages.label: KRB_AP_REP (15)
messages.note: Optional proof of the server's identity (mutual authentication).

data.title: KDC-REQ-BODY (ASN.1, abridged from RFC 4120 section 5.4.1)
data.code:
AS-REQ   ::= [APPLICATION 10] KDC-REQ
TGS-REQ  ::= [APPLICATION 12] KDC-REQ

KDC-REQ ::= SEQUENCE {
    pvno     [1] INTEGER (5),
    msg-type [2] INTEGER (10 -- AS -- | 12 -- TGS --),
    padata   [3] SEQUENCE OF PA-DATA OPTIONAL,
    req-body [4] KDC-REQ-BODY
}

KDC-REQ-BODY ::= SEQUENCE {
    kdc-options [0] KDCOptions,
    cname       [1] PrincipalName OPTIONAL,  -- AS-REQ only
    realm       [2] Realm,
    sname       [3] PrincipalName OPTIONAL,
    from        [4] KerberosTime OPTIONAL,
    till        [5] KerberosTime,
    rtime       [6] KerberosTime OPTIONAL,
    nonce       [7] UInt32,
    etype       [8] SEQUENCE OF Int32,       -- in preference order
    addresses   [9] HostAddresses OPTIONAL,
    ...
}

cells: Service ticket and service session key

viz.caption: Checks the server makes on an AP-REQ

items.title: Can I open the ticket?
items.text: The server decrypts it with its own key. Failure means the ticket was not issued for this service.

items.title: Does the authenticator match?
items.text: The client name and realm in the authenticator must match the ticket (KRB_AP_ERR_BADMATCH otherwise).

items.title: Is the clock close enough?
items.text: ctime must be within the allowed skew, typically 5 minutes (KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW).

items.title: Is this a replay?
items.text: The server remembers recent authenticators and rejects a duplicate (KRB_AP_ERR_REPEAT).

layers.label: Application data
layers.detail: Protected only if the application uses KRB_PRIV, KRB_SAFE or its own protection

layers.label: Authenticator and AP exchange
layers.detail: Proves the client holds the session key, with replay detection from timestamps and a replay cache

layers.label: Tickets from the KDC
layers.detail: Authenticated, time-limited credentials sealed in the service's key

layers.label: UDP or TCP port 88
layers.detail: No confidentiality for the exchange itself; ticket contents such as names are visible

today: Kerberos Version 5 is widely deployed. It is the default authentication protocol in Microsoft Active Directory domains and is used by MIT Kerberos and Heimdal on Unix and Linux. Hadoop and many other enterprise systems also rely on it. Applications usually reach it through GSS-API (RFC 4121) or SASL rather than calling it directly. RFC 4120 has since been updated by a number of later RFCs; for example RFC 6649 deprecates DES and other weak algorithms that this document still lists as SHOULD.
